---
title: "Methods and how to tune them"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8,
                      fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 96, message = FALSE,
                      warning = FALSE)
has_mofa <- requireNamespace("MOFA2", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("reticulate", quietly = TRUE) &&
  isTRUE(tryCatch(reticulate::py_module_available("mofapy2"),
                  error = function(e) FALSE))
```

```{r}
library(factomics)
sim <- simulate_multiomics(n_samples = 60, seed = 1)
```

All methods are called the same way, through `run_factor_pipeline(X, methods, k)`.
Method-specific settings are ordinary arguments with a method prefix
(`fabia_*`, `mofa_*`, `gfa_*`, `pca_*`, `sgcca_*`, `jive_*`).

```{r}
knitr::kable(list_factor_methods()[, c("method", "package", "family",
                                      "description")])
```

## Preprocessing shared by all methods

By default (`scale_features = TRUE`) every feature is z-scored, so all features
start on the same footing, and zero-variance features are set to zero. Samples
are aligned across views by name. If your data are already normalised the way
you want, use `scale_features = FALSE`.

## PCA: block-weighted, concatenated

The simplest integrative baseline: the views are stacked and a single PCA is
run. With `pca_block_weight = TRUE` (default) each view is divided by the square
root of its number of features, so a view with 10,000 genes does not swamp a view
with 50 metabolites. It needs nothing beyond base R.

```{r}
res_pca <- run_factor_pipeline(sim$data, methods = "PCA", k = 4,
                               verbose = FALSE)
round(res_pca$PCA$meta$variance_percent, 1)
```

## MFA: Multiple Factor Analysis

MFA (FactoMineR) weights each view by its first eigenvalue, then runs a global
PCA. It is fast, deterministic and a strong default. It needs at least two views.
`mfa_group_sizes` can override the grouping of columns.

## FABIA

FABIA is a sparse, biclustering-oriented factor model: each factor is driven by a
small set of features and a subset of samples. `fabia_alpha` controls loading
sparseness (larger = sparser), `fabia_cyc` the number of iterations.

```{r}
res_fabia <- run_factor_pipeline(sim$data, methods = "FABIA", k = 4,
                                 fabia_alpha = 0.05, fabia_cyc = 500,
                                 verbose = FALSE)
```

## GFA: Group Factor Analysis

GFA is a Bayesian factor model with view-wise sparsity: each factor can be active
in all views, in some, or in only one. `gfa_iter_burnin` and `gfa_iter_max`
control the Gibbs sampler. More iterations give more stable factors.

## MOFA2

MOFA2 is a Bayesian framework for multi-omics factor analysis that handles
missing values and different likelihoods. It runs in Python (`mofapy2`) via
reticulate. Either install `mofapy2` and tell factomics where that Python is:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
run_factor_pipeline(sim$data, methods = "MOFA", k = 4,
                    mofa_python = "/usr/bin/python3")
```

or let MOFA2 build its own Python environment with
`mofa_use_basilisk = TRUE`. The Docker image has everything set up already.
`mofa_convergence` (`"fast"`, `"medium"`, `"slow"`) trades speed for precision.

```{r, eval = has_mofa}
res_mofa <- run_factor_pipeline(sim$data, methods = "MOFA", k = 4,
                                mofa_convergence = "fast", verbose = FALSE)
res_mofa$MOFA$plots$variance_by_factor
```

## SGCCA: sparse generalised CCA

SGCCA (mixOmics) finds components that maximise the covariance between views,
one component per view and dimension; factomics reports their average as the
sample score. By default all features are kept; `sgcca_keep` gives the number of
features to keep per view and component, for sparse, more interpretable loadings.

```{r}
res_sgcca <- run_factor_pipeline(sim$data, methods = "SGCCA", k = 3,
                                 sgcca_keep = c(30, 15, 10), verbose = FALSE)
colSums(res_sgcca$SGCCA$loadings != 0)
```

## JIVE

JIVE splits each view into a **joint** part shared by all views (rank `k`), an
**individual** part specific to the view (rank `jive_rank_individual`) and noise.
factomics reports the factors of the joint part; the individual parts are kept in
`meta$individual`.

```{r}
res_jive <- run_factor_pipeline(sim$data, methods = "JIVE", k = 3,
                                jive_rank_individual = 1, verbose = FALSE)
```

## RABFA: graph-guided Bayesian factor analysis

RABFA (Zhang, Chang, Shen and Long, 2024, *Biometrics*) is a Bayesian factor
model that uses prior knowledge of which features act together, typically a
pathway graph such as KEGG, to guide which loadings are shrunk to zero:

- every loading has its own Laplace shrinkage parameter, so strong signals are
  shrunk little and noise a lot (**adaptive shrinkage**);
- the log shrinkage parameters of features that are connected in the graph are
  correlated through a sparse precision matrix that is itself learnt from the
  data, so connected features tend to be selected together, while edges that
  disagree with the data are down-weighted (**robust to wrong edges**).

factomics implements the Gaussian version of the model with a Gibbs sampler
(Metropolis-Hastings for the shrinkage parameters, block Gibbs for the graph
precision matrix), written from the published model.

The graph is a data frame of edges with columns `from` and `to`, an adjacency
matrix, or one adjacency matrix per view. Feature names may be plain (`TP53`)
or view-prefixed (`rna::TP53`); edges between different views are ignored, as
in the paper. Here we build the graph that the simulation actually used, by
connecting the features loaded on the same true factor:

```{r}
W <- sim$truth$W
pathways <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(W), function(v)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(ncol(W[[v]])), function(f) {
    on <- rownames(W[[v]])[W[[v]][, f] != 0]
    data.frame(from = on[1], to = on[-1], view = v)   # star-shaped pathway
  }))))
edges <- data.frame(from = paste0(pathways$view, "::", pathways$from),
                    to   = paste0(pathways$view, "::", pathways$to))
head(edges, 3)
```

```{r}
res_rabfa <- run_factor_pipeline(sim$data, methods = "RABFA", k = 4,
                                 rabfa_graph = edges,
                                 rabfa_iter = 1500, rabfa_burnin = 750,
                                 verbose = FALSE)
res_rabfa$RABFA$meta$n_edges
```

The result has the usual `scores` and `loadings` (posterior means) and, in
`meta`, the loadings whose 95% credible interval excludes zero, the posterior
shrinkage parameters, a BIC-type criterion, and the log-likelihood trace for
checking convergence:

```{r, fig.height = 3}
m <- res_rabfa$RABFA$meta
colSums(m$selected)
plot(m$loglik_trace, type = "l", xlab = "Iteration", ylab = "Log-likelihood",
     main = "RABFA trace (burn-in = first half)")
```

How well do the selected loadings match the true signal features?

```{r}
truth <- sim$truth$feature_labels[rownames(m$selected)]
table(selected = rowSums(m$selected) > 0, true_signal = truth)
```

Without pathway knowledge, `build_feature_graph()` gives a data-driven graph
(features in the same view with high correlation), and `rabfa()` is a shortcut:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
g   <- build_feature_graph(sim$data, cutoff = 0.5, max_neighbors = 5)
fit <- rabfa(sim$data, k = 4, graph = g, iter = 5000, burnin = 2500)
```

The main tuning parameters (`rabfa_control()`) are `nu1` (overall shrinkage;
larger is sparser) and `nu2` (how adaptive each loading's shrinkage is); the
paper chose them, and `k`, by grid search on the BIC stored in `meta$bic`.
`eta = 10` and `eps = 0.2` follow the paper. MCMC needs enough iterations: the
paper used 5,000-10,000; check `loglik_trace` has flattened after burn-in.

## Running many methods together

If a method fails (missing package, too few views, numerical problem) it is
skipped with a warning and the others are still returned. Use
`stop_on_error = TRUE` to make failures fatal instead.

```{r}
res_all <- run_factor_pipeline(
  sim$data, methods = c("PCA", "MFA", "FABIA", "GFA", "SGCCA", "JIVE",
                       "RABFA"),
  k = 4, rabfa_graph = edges, rabfa_iter = 1000, rabfa_burnin = 500,
  verbose = FALSE)
res_all
```

```{r, fig.height = 3.4}
plot_variance_explained(res_all, type = "total")
```

## Choosing the number of factors

There is no single right `k`. A practical approach is to fit a generous `k`,
look at `plot_variance_explained()`, and keep the factors that explain a
noticeable share of variance in at least one view, or that associate with
covariates of interest (`plot_factor_associations()`).
